title: Senior's toolkit: searching and sorting in .NET
summary: BinarySearch and its ~index, stable versus unstable sorts, comparers, and when not to sort at all.

steps.title: Senior's toolkit: searching and sorting in .NET
steps.body: At work you call the framework's sort and search; you do not write them. What experienced developers know is their contracts: which sort is stable, what `BinarySearch` returns when it misses, and how strings compare.

toolkit.what: O(log n) search in sorted data (also `List<T>.BinarySearch`). When the value is missing it returns a negative number: the bitwise complement of where it would go.
flags: not found; `~index` is the insertion point that keeps it sorted
the data must be sorted with the comparer you search with
toolkit.example:
int i = list.BinarySearch(x);
if (i < 0) list.Insert(~i, x);   // keep the list sorted

toolkit.what: In-place introsort, O(n log n), and **not stable**: items that compare equal may swap. `List<T>.Sort` is the same.
flags: sort two arrays together by the first
toolkit.example: orders.Sort((a, b) => a.Date.CompareTo(b.Date) is var c && c != 0 ? c : a.Id.CompareTo(b.Id));

toolkit.what: LINQ sorting: **stable**, returns a new sequence, and runs when enumerated. Use it when equal items must keep their order or you need several keys.
flags: materialise once if you enumerate the result more than once

toolkit.what: Sorting strings uses the current culture by default, which can differ between machines. For keys, ids and anything machine-readable, compare ordinally.
flags: by character code; fast and the same everywhere
toolkit.example:
Array.Sort(skus, StringComparer.Ordinal);
var byLength = Comparer<string>.Create((a, b) => a.Length.CompareTo(b.Length));

toolkit.what: The best item in one O(n) pass (.NET 6+). Sorting just to take the first element is O(n log n) and allocates.
flags: the item with the largest key, not the key
MaxBy returns null for reference types; `Max` on an empty sequence of value types throws

steps.explain: 25 is missing; it belongs at index 2 (between 20 and 30). `BinarySearch` returns `~2`, which is `-3`, and `~(-3)` gives the insertion point back.

steps.prompt: `OrderBy` is stable. What does this print?
steps.explain: Items with the same age keep their original order: Bob before Dee, Ann before Cid. `Array.Sort` makes no such promise.

steps.prompt: To save allocations, someone replaced `rows.OrderBy(r => r.Date).ToList()` with `rows.Sort((a, b) => a.Date.CompareTo(b.Date))`. Since then, a snapshot test of the report fails now and then: rows with the same date appear in a different order. What is the fix?
options: `List.Sort` is unstable. Add a tie-breaker to the comparison (`... : a.Id.CompareTo(b.Id)`), or go back to `OrderBy`
Seed the random number generator before sorting
steps.explain: Equal keys have no defined order in an unstable sort. A total order (a unique tie-breaker) makes the result deterministic with any sort; `OrderBy` keeps the input order for ties.

steps.prompt: Match each call to the right description.
pairs: in place, O(n log n), not stable
one O(n) pass for the best item

steps.prompt: Insert a price into a sorted list so that it stays sorted.
steps.explain: `IndexOf` is a linear scan and returns `-1` without an insertion point. `-i` is off by one: `~i` equals `-i - 1`.

steps.title: Make it a habit
steps.body: When sorting, ask in review: does the order of ties matter, and are strings compared ordinally? Use `MaxBy`/`MinBy` instead of sorting for one item, and `BinarySearch` with `~index` to keep a list sorted as you insert.
